newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Filipino defence chief launches presidential bid.
newsitem.headline: Filipino defence chief launches presidential bid.

text.p: Philippine Defence Secretary Renato de Villa launched his candidacy for president on Sunday, joining a dozen others, including a popular former movie star, in a scramble to succeed President Fidel Ramos.
"I will not beat around the bush. I accept the challenge," de Villa told 5,000 supporters in a rally in his nearby home province of Batangas timed to coincide with his 62nd birthday.
"Who can turn his back on this public clamour?" he said.
Although the presidential election, in May, 1998, is still 10 months away, at least a dozen aspirants are already touring the country to strengthen their grassroots support.
De Villa, a former army general who has fared badly in popularity polls, is one of seven members of the administration Lakas party who have signified their intention to run.
They will fight for the party's nomination at its national convention to be held in November or December.
Ramos, whose six-year term ends in June next year, is constitutionally barred from running for a second term.
Widely regarded as the front-runner in the race is Vice-President Joseph "Erap" Estrada, who counts on his huge appeal as a former action star in local movies.
The others include opposition senator Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo, Ramos's sister, senator Leticia Shahani and Lower House Speaker Jose de Venecia.

Ramos met the seven Lakas "presidentiables" on Friday and offered to train them at "the job of being president" by working with him at the presidential palace for a specific period, a Lakas announcement said.
Although the party bet will be officially picked by a convention, Lakas said it had asked Ramos to publicly endorse his own choice, reducing the convention to a mere formality.
Despite having a powerful nationwide political machinery, Lakas faces a dilemma in that all its seven aspirants, from de Villa to de Ocampo and de Venecia rate poorly in opinion surveys.
Estrada has consistently topped the surveys, with Arroyo and another opposition senator, Miriam Santiago, behind him.

"Lakas has the strongest political machine...but the intra-party free-for-all, in which no one is showing a high popularity rating, reduces Lakas's advantage," political analyst Amando Doronila wrote in the Philippine Daily Inquirer newspaper.
